children.text: President Clinton's health plan was widely discussed, with Latino/a health advocates noting that as many as one-third of Latino/as lacked health coverage and stood to benefit significantly from reform. However, the Hispanic Medical Association, representing 25 Latino/a health groups, expressed concern that the plan excluded undocumented workers, failed to adequately address border healthcare as a bi-national issue, and did not ensure cultural and linguistic access for the country's 24 million Latino/as. Mexican President Carlos Salinas visited San Francisco to promote NAFTA, arguing that free trade would reduce illegal immigration by creating jobs in Mexico, and pushing back against characterizations of undocumented workers as a burden on U.S. taxpayers. Missouri Congressman Richard Gephardt's announced opposition to NAFTA was seen as a significant setback for the treaty's prospects in Congress. California State Senator Art Torres called for a cooling-off period on all immigration-related legislation, arguing the debate had become too emotional and that immigration needed to be addressed as a complex international issue. In El Paso, the Border Patrol launched Operation Blockade, deploying hundreds of agents along 20 miles of the U.S.-Mexico border in a round-the-clock effort. Officials reported a 90% drop in arrests of undocumented immigrants, but immigration rights advocates warned the operation created an atmosphere of fear in border communities.

Correspondent Patricia Guadalupe provided an in-depth look at the healthcare plan's implications for Latino/as. A notable provision would equalize Medicaid payments for Puerto Rico with the mainland for the first time, bringing the island from 20% of standard coverage to full parity, which Puerto Rico's resident commissioner, Carlos Romero Barcelo, praised as historic. However, the plan's exclusion of undocumented workers drew sharp criticism from Cecilia Munoz of the National Council of La Raza, who described it as politically motivated and harmful to public health. Chief presidential advisor Ira Magaziner defended the exclusion on the grounds that benefits should be reserved for legal residents. Republican responses were generally more favorable to Clinton's plan than usual, though some raised concerns about bureaucracy.
National Professor of the Year: Dr. Vicente Villa

Maria Martin spoke with Dr. Vicente Domingo Villa of Southwestern University in Georgetown, Texas, named National Professor of the Year by the Council for the Advancement and Support of Education. Dr. Villa described how, when he arrived at Southwestern in 1985, there were virtually no Latino/a science students. Eight years later, nearly 20% of science graduates were Hispanic. He credited informal weekly study sessions outside the classroom as the key to building real relationships with students and spotting those who were not aiming high enough. The son of a ranch cowboy who never attended school and a mother who emigrated from Monterrey, Mexico, with a fifth-grade education, Dr. Villa described parental encouragement as the foundation of educational achievement, and said his father's difficult wartime experience as a non-English speaker had made education the defining value of his household.
The Border Fence Debate in Arizona

Reporter Manuel Arcadia covered community forums in Naco, Arizona, over a Border Patrol proposal to build steel walls along portions of the Arizona-Mexico border. Supporters, including the local trade alliance, argued the barrier was needed to deter drug traffickers and unauthorized crossings. Opponents from the coalition Hermanos Unidos called the wall racist, noting no such barrier would be proposed on the Canadian border. One activist compared any aesthetically designed version of the wall to a beautiful Berlin Wall, rejecting the premise entirely. The proposal had already been rejected in Douglas, Arizona, and was under reconsideration in Nogales, with Naco still deliberating.
The Year of the White Bear

Correspondent Betto Arcos reported on a multimedia art exhibition at the Otis Gallery in Los Angeles, curated by Coco Fusco and performance artist Guillermo Gomez-Pena. Titled The Year of the White Bear, the show took its name from a Colombian Indigenous term for Europeans and used performance, visual art, ceramics, and audio installations to interrogate 500 years of colonialism and its connections to contemporary issues, including NAFTA, immigration enforcement, and the INS. Gomez-Pena argued that political art need not be solemn, and that humor was often a more effective vehicle for political reflection. The show juxtaposed pre-Hispanic imagery with current events, inviting visitors to consider how the history of conquest continues to shape present-day power and policy.
